Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Stratosphere Dynamics Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, the Q&A session will follow the standard operator instructions. Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Stratosphere Dynamics' Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today are Johnathan Reyes, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Lang, Chief Financial Officer; Patricia Gomez, Chief Operating Officer; Dr. Raj Singh, Chief Technology Officer; and Emily Carter, Chief Strategy Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Please refer to our SEC filings, including our most recent Form 10-K and 10-Q, for a complete discussion of risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied.

Johnathan Reyes:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Stratosphere Dynamics delivered a solid performance in Q3, demonstrating the resilience of our business model and the strength of our diversified portfolio across defense, space, and commercial aerospace. Our priorities remain focused on executing our strategy, driving operational excellence, and delivering long-term value to our shareholders. Today, we'll cover key areas including program margins and cost performance, expansion of our service offerings and customer base, R&D investments in next-generation platforms, revenue and earnings guidance by segment, free cash flow generation and utilization, and major new contract awards.

We are particularly excited about the recent advancements in our Next-Generation Air Dominance program and its potential to drive multi-year growth through air dominance superiority. We are seeing strong demand for our defense systems, and our commercial aerospace business is recovering steadily amid rising global travel.

With that, I'll turn it over to Michael for the financial details.

Michael Lang:
Thank you, Johnathan. Now, let's turn to the financials. In Q3, we reported revenue of $6.5 billion, representing a 12% increase year-over-year, driven by robust execution across our segments. Our adjusted earnings per share were $1.85, exceeding expectations. We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet with $5.0 billion in cash and equivalents and low net debt leverage. Our guidance for the full year remains unchanged at $26-27 billion in revenue and adjusted EPS of $7.50-$7.80. We are actively managing our costs amid inflationary pressures while investing in key growth initiatives like hypersonics and digital sustainment. We are also focused on returning capital to shareholders through our dividend, now at $1.20 annually, and $2 billion in share repurchases this year.

Our specific financial highlights include gross margin of 22.8%, up 110 basis points sequentially; operating income of $975 million; and free cash flow of $850 million.

As we dive deeper into our Aerospace & Defense segment, which represents 65% of our total revenue this quarter at $4.2 billion, let me focus on program margins and cost performance analysis. This remains a cornerstone of our financial health, given the long-cycle nature of our programs and the fixed-price incentive contracts that dominate our $52 billion funded backlog—up 8% year-over-year.

The headline is that segment program margins expanded 70 basis points sequentially to 10.8% in Q3, marking our strongest quarterly performance since the F-35 Lot 15 low-rate initial production ramp in 2021. This compares favorably to our full-year 2023 average of 9.9% and outperforms peers like Lockheed Martin’s Aeronautics segment, which reported 10.1% in their latest quarter amid similar supply chain headwinds. Year-to-date, we're at 10.4%, putting us on track for our guided 10-11% full-year range.

This margin expansion was driven by disciplined cost management, favorable contract mix, and proactive risk retirement. Our Cost Performance Index averaged 1.06 across the portfolio—meaning we're delivering 6% under our latest Estimate at Completion baselines—while our Schedule Performance Index held steady at 0.98, reflecting minor slips on a few international deliveries due to export licensing delays. A CPI north of 1.0 is rare in our industry, especially with inflation-adjusted labor and material costs up 5-7% industry-wide per Deloitte's latest A&D outlook.

Breaking it down by key programs: On the Next-Generation Air Dominance Fighter Program, margins came in at 11.5%, up from 10.8% last quarter, fueled by $1.2 billion in low-rate initial production funding from the U.S. Air Force. We've retired 85% of our engineering change order risks through digital twin simulations, reducing non-recurring engineering costs by 12% versus our initial bid. Cost performance is exemplary with a CPI of 1.12, thanks to our additive manufacturing initiative for titanium engine components, which shaved 15% off airframe unit costs.

For the Hypersonic Strike Missile Family, this program's 9.7% margin reflects a healthy mix of U.S. DoD prime contracts and Foreign Military Sales to Australia and Poland under the AUKUS pillar two framework. We've seen $800 million in new awards this quarter, boosting our book-to-bill to 1.3x. CPI stands at 1.04, with overruns contained on solid rocket motor procurement through dual-sourcing from Northrop Grumman and our in-house facilities. Inflation passthrough clauses on these cost-plus-incentive-fee contracts protected us from the 22% titanium price surge tied to Russian sanctions.

Commercial Crew and Space Mobility Programs saw margins at 7.9%, pressured by NASA certification delays on our Orion successor vehicle, similar to Boeing's Starliner challenges. However, we've improved from 6.5% in Q2 through aggressive labor productivity gains—up 18% via our 'AeroSmart' AI-driven workforce optimization tool. CPI is now 0.97, with EAC adjustments complete on the first 12 vehicles. Positively, our $2.4 billion commercial satellite constellation backlog with OneWeb-like customers is accretive at 12% margins, diversifying away from government-heavy exposure.

Regionally, U.S. programs drove 72% of segment revenue, with margins at 11.2% benefiting from the FY24 NDAA's 4.5% topline growth and supplemental Ukraine aid funding our precision-guided munitions ramp. International margins were 9.2%, tempered by FX headwinds in Europe—the euro's 3% depreciation versus the dollar eroded $45 million in FMS value—but offset by strong Middle East demand for our HSM variants amid Red Sea tensions. In Asia-Pacific, AUKUS and Quad partner awards added $600 million to backlog, with margins trending toward 11% as we localize final assembly in Australia to comply with ITAR offsets.

Strategically, our margin performance underscores three key initiatives. First, supply chain resilience: We've derisked 92% of our critical tier-1 suppliers—think Collins Aerospace for avionics and Raytheon for seekers—through a 'China-plus-one' strategy, reducing lead times by 25% and locking in multi-year titanium offtake agreements at FY23 prices. Second, digital transformation: Our enterprise-wide PLM system, integrated with Siemens Teamcenter, has enabled real-time EAC forecasting, cutting variance by 30% on fixed-price development contracts. Third, pricing discipline: On new bids, we're incorporating 4-6% annual escalators for labor and materials, informed by Blue Origin and SpaceX competitive dynamics, which has won us share in the hypersonic market projected to grow at 18% CAGR through 2030 per Teal Group.

Looking forward, we expect Q4 margins to hold in the 10.5-11% range, with upside from NGAD LRIP acceleration and HSM export deliveries. Risks remain around DoD budget sequestration talks and potential U.S. government shutdowns, but our CPIF-heavy portfolio—55% of backlog—provides a natural hedge. Funded backlog conversion remains strong at 22% this year, supporting 5-7% organic growth in 2025.

Turning to another key growth driver, our strategic expansion of service offerings and customer base. The Aerospace & Defense sector is undergoing a profound shift toward services-led revenue models, with high-margin sustainment, digital engineering, and mission assurance contracts now accounting for over 40% of industry bookings, per Deloitte's latest A&D outlook. We're capitalizing on this trend aggressively, delivering 28% year-over-year growth in our Services segment to $512 million in Q3, representing 32% of total revenue—up from 24% a year ago. This expansion not only diversifies our revenue streams but also builds a more resilient backlog, now standing at $3.2 billion, with 65% weighted toward multi-year IDIQ and FMS sustainment awards.

Traditionally, we've been a leader in tactical missile systems and C4ISR avionics, akin to our peers at Raytheon and L3Harris. But we've pivoted decisively into next-generation services, launching our "DynSustain" platform earlier this year—a suite of AI-enabled predictive maintenance and digital twin solutions tailored for legacy fleets like the F-16 and AH-64 Apache. This initiative leverages our proprietary PHM algorithms, which have reduced unscheduled maintenance events by 22% in beta trials with the U.S. Army's Aviation Branch. We've secured three major OTAs totaling $280 million for DynSustain integration on Joint Light Tactical Vehicles and MQ-9 Reaper UAS platforms, with margins expanding to 68%—well above our legacy product mix of 18%.

Complementing this, we're ramping additive manufacturing services through our new AM Center of Excellence in Huntsville, Alabama, co-located with the DoD's DIU ecosystem. This allows rapid prototyping of hypersonic components, such as thermal protection systems for programs like DARPA's HAWC, cutting lead times by 45% and enabling just-in-time supply for primes like Lockheed Martin on the NGAD pathway. We've also entered the space domain with SDA services, including orbital debris tracking via our partnership with LeoLabs, securing a $95 million NRO contract for GEO satellite sustainment.

On the customer base front, diversification is our north star. We've expanded from our core U.S. DoD footprint—still 72% of services revenue—to 28 international and commercial customers, adding 22 net-new relationships this quarter alone. This includes breakthrough FMS awards: a $450 million, 5-year sustainment deal with the Polish Air Force for Black Hawk MRO, capitalizing on Europe's $100 billion-plus rearmament post-Ukraine; and a $210 million IDIQ with the Indian Navy for P-8I maritime patrol upgrades, strengthening our Indo-Pacific presence amid AUKUS and QUAD dynamics.

Regionally, Europe now drives 19% of our services bookings, up from 8% last year, fueled by NATO's 2% GDP pledges and urgent needs for Ukraine aid sustainment—think Javelin missile logistics mirroring RTX's recent wins. In the Middle East, we're at 12% penetration, with a UAE GHF depot-level repair contract worth $150 million, hedging against oil volatility while tapping into the $50 billion regional MRO market projected by Frost & Sullivan. Asia-Pacific is our fastest grower at 35% YoY, with new sustainment pacts in Australia and Japan for F-35 ALC support, positioning us ahead of geopolitical flashpoints like the Taiwan Strait.

Strategically, this expansion de-risks our model by shifting to 75% recurring revenue in services, with LTV per platform exceeding $500 million over 10-15 years—far outpacing one-off hardware sales. We're mitigating ITAR constraints through hybrid JVs, like our 40% stake in AeroDef Asia Pte Ltd in Singapore, which facilitates tech transfer for allies without full export licensing. Margins here are holding at 65-72%, bolstered by labor efficiencies from our $120 million investment in Industry 4.0 automation.

Looking forward, we see services scaling to 40% of revenue by FY25, with a $1.2 billion pipeline including hypersonic test range services and counter-UAS sustainment for the Army's LTAMDS.

Next, on our R&D investments, which remain a cornerstone of our long-term growth strategy in the Aerospace & Defense sector. In fiscal year 2024, we deployed $2.8 billion in research and development—up 18% year-over-year and representing 9.2% of our total revenue, in line with industry peers like Northrop Grumman at around 9% and Lockheed Martin at 7.5%. This includes both independent research and development funding of $450 million, which gives us strategic flexibility, and customer-funded efforts tied to major primes like the U.S. Air Force's Next Generation Air Dominance program and the Navy's Collaborative Combat Aircraft initiatives.

Breaking it down by key focus areas, where we're prioritizing next-generation platforms and enabling technologies to address the evolving threat landscape driven by great power competition—particularly in the Indo-Pacific against peer adversaries like China's J-20 fleet and Russia's Kinzhal hypersonics.

Our largest allocation continues to be in advanced air dominance platforms at 38% of R&D spend, or $1.06 billion. We've accelerated maturation of our digital engineering twin for a NGAD-family Penetrating Counter-Air demonstrator, achieving Milestone B readiness ahead of schedule. This builds on our Block 4 F-35 sustainment work with Lockheed, where we've integrated AI-driven sensor fusion that reduces pilot workload by 40% in simulated contested environments. On the unmanned side, $320 million went into CCA risk reduction, partnering with the Air Force Research Laboratory on loyal wingman architectures. Early flight tests of our XQ-58A Valkyrie derivative showed 95% autonomy in beyond-visual-range engagements, positioning us for the $6 billion CCA spiral development contract expected in FY25. Regionally, this aligns with Indo-Pacific Command's pivot: 60% of our air platform R&D is tailored for Pacific theater ops, including conformal fuel tanks for extended range against A2/AD bubbles and low-observable materials resilient to directed energy weapons.

Hypersonics remain a high-priority disruptor, with 22% of R&D or $616 million, including $250 million in boost-glide and scramjet propulsion maturation. Our AGM-183A ARRW-equivalent air-launched rapid response weapon completed end-to-end hot-fire tests at Mach 12, achieving a 75% cost reduction per unit via 3D-printed solid rocket motors—a breakthrough we're scaling for the Army's Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon. We've also invested in ground-launched hypersonics for European allies under AUKUS Pillar II, where UK and Australian co-development could unlock $1.2 billion in export opportunities by 2028. Trends here are clear: DoD hypersonic funding surged 25% to $4.7 billion in FY24, but supply chain bottlenecks in rare earths for thermal protection systems have pushed timelines. Our strategic hedge? A $100 million materials science IRAD line for carbon-carbon composites, partnering with RTX on next-gen seekers.

We're doubling down on advanced propulsion and directed energy at 15% of R&D, or $420 million. This includes $180 million advancing our XA102 adaptive cycle engine variant—delivering 30% better thrust-specific fuel consumption than the F135 baseline for 6th-gen platforms. This supports the Air Force's Engine Prototype Demonstration and positions us against GE's XA100 in downselects. In directed energy, 25 megawatt-class solid-state lasers for high-energy laser ship defense hit 50% efficiency milestones, funded via ONR's directed energy roadmap. Middle East deployments with CENTCOM partners validated counter-UAV efficacy, burning out Group 3 drones at 5 km—critical amid Houthi threats.

Finally, C4ISR, autonomy, and space resilience capture 25% of R&D, or $700 million. $280 million fueled Joint All-Domain Command and Control integration, including mesh networking for Starlink-like proliferated low-Earth orbit constellations. Our digital twin simulations reduced integration risks by 35% for ABMS Increment 2. Autonomy R&D hit $150 million, with AI/ML algorithms for human-machine teaming certified at TRL 7 under DARPA's Air Combat Evolution program. Space investments—$170 million—target resilient SATCOM, countering China's ASAT threats. We're maturing optical inter-satellite links for the Space Development Agency's Transport Layer Tranche 2, with first-launch slots booked for Q3 FY25.

These investments aren't just spend—they're force multipliers. Our R&D return on investment model projects a 3.5x payback over 10 years, driven by 65% customer funding capture rates and a robust $45 billion bid pipeline. We're mitigating sequestration risks from the FY25 NDAA caps by diversifying: 40% U.S. DoD, 25% international with NATO's €100B+ rearmament, 20% space/commercial like NASA CLPS lunar landers, and 15% classified black programs. Geopolitically, NATO's 2% GDP pledge and Ukraine's demonstrated need for attritable munitions are tailwinds—our drone swarm tech could capture 15% of the $10B global loitering munition market by 2027. Risks include talent shortages, though we're up 12% in hiring PhDs from MIT and GA Tech, and inflation on exotics like gallium nitride semiconductors, up 22% YoY. Looking ahead, we expect FY25 R&D to grow 12-15% to $3.2-$3.3 billion, with 20% IRAD upside from SBIR Phase III transitions. This positions Stratosphere Dynamics at the forefront of multi-domain superiority.

Before moving on, let me provide our detailed FY2025 revenue and earnings guidance by segment, reflecting disciplined execution amid a dynamic macroeconomic and geopolitical landscape. Our book-to-bill ratio stood at 1.15x at quarter-end, with a record $128 billion backlog—up 8% year-over-year—providing strong visibility. We're guiding total company revenue to $92-95 billion for FY2025, a 10-14% increase from FY2024's $83.7 billion, with adjusted segment operating margins expanding 50-100 basis points to 11.5-12.0%. This incorporates ongoing supply chain normalization, labor cost inflation at mid-single digits offset by productivity gains from our LEAN+ digital transformation initiative, and favorable program mix.

By segment, starting with Defense Platforms, which represented 42% of Q3 revenue: We're guiding revenue to $40-42 billion, up 12-16% year-over-year, driven by accelerated deliveries on our Next Generation Air Dominance demonstrator program—akin to the Air Force's CCA initiatives—and sustained F-35 Lot 18 production ramp. Expect 220-240 fighter/attack aircraft deliveries, including 120 F-35s for U.S. and allied customers, with international sales comprising 35% of the mix, boosted by FMS deals in the Middle East and Indo-Pacific. Margins are projected at 10.8-11.3%, up from 10.1% in FY2024, reflecting fixed-price contract efficiencies and lower learning curve costs on our proprietary adaptive engine tech, similar to GE's XA100 but integrated into NGAD. Key risks include titanium supply constraints from Ukraine-related disruptions, but our dual-sourcing with domestic mills mitigates this. Strategically, we're positioning for the FY2025 DoD budget's $180 billion procurement topline, with early wins on hypersonic boost-glide vehicles for the Army's LRHW program.

Moving to Missiles & Fire Control, our highest-margin segment at 38% of Q3 revenue: Revenue guidance is $28-30 billion, a robust 15-20% growth, fueled by replenishment orders post-Ukraine and Red Sea operations. We're forecasting 4,500-5,000 all-up-round deliveries, including 2,200 JASSM-ERs and 1,500 PAC-3 MSE interceptors, with production rates hitting 120 units per month by Q4. International demand from NATO allies—up 25%—supports this, alongside hypersonic effectors like our HAWC-derived scramjet prototypes. Adjusted operating margins expand to 14.5-15.0%, from 13.8% last year, thanks to scale on the PrSM program and value engineering on Stinger Block I upgrades. Bookings remain strong at $35 billion YTD, with a 1.3x book-to-bill. Geopolitical tensions in the Taiwan Strait are accelerating allied investments in stand-off weapons, positioning us ahead of competitors like MBDA.

Next, Space & Airborne Systems, 15% of Q3 revenue, where we're capitalizing on the new space race: Expect $14-15 billion in revenue, up 8-12%, with growth split evenly between classified DoD satellites and commercial constellations. Key drivers include 12 GPS IIIF launches for the Space Force, our role in the NSSL Phase 3 fleet competing with SpaceX's Starshield, and proliferated LEO architectures for missile warning—think 50+ SDA Tranche 2 satellites. Commercial side sees uplift from imaging payloads for Maxar's WorldView successors and hosted payloads on Blue Origin's New Glenn. Margins guide to 11.0-11.5%, improving on supply chain debottlenecking for gallium nitride RF components. Regionally, Asia-Pacific growth at 20% reflects AUKUS pillar-two workshares, while Europe benefits from €100 billion EU defense spending hike. Our digital engineering pivot—using MBSE tools like Cameo—has de-risked five IR&D programs, enhancing our edge in resilient, disaggregated space.

Finally, Commercial Aviation & Services, 5% of Q3 but with outsized growth potential: Revenue to $10-12 billion, surging 25-40% on OEM recovery and MRO expansion. Narrowbody ramp includes 350-400 deliveries of our 737MAX-equivalent ApexJet family, with lessor orders from Avolon and SMBC ramping to 15/month. Widebody aftermarket services grow 18%, driven by GTF engine overhauls addressing Pratt & Whitney's durability issues via our ceramic matrix composite upgrades and sustainable aviation fuel certification on 787 derivatives. Margins at 9.5-10.0%, up from breakeven in FY2024, as we lap COVID-era disruptions. Boeing's recent FAA validations inform our quality gates, ensuring 99.5% on-time delivery. Regional note: China OEM exposure at 15% accelerates with COMAC C919 integration, while India’s IndiGo fleet expansion adds tailwinds.

In summary, this guidance embeds $2.5-3.0 billion in net favorable program adjustments, conservative DoD funding assumptions at 95% of the $850 billion topline request, and 4-5% organic growth ex-FX. Free cash flow guides to $6.5-7.5 billion, supporting $4 billion in dividends and buybacks. We're well-positioned for multi-year tailwinds: U.S. supplemental budgets, NATO 2%+ pledges, and commercial traffic at 105% of 2019 levels per IATA.

On free cash flow generation and utilization, which continues to be a cornerstone of our financial strength and strategic flexibility: For the quarter, we generated $850 million in free cash flow, bringing our year-to-date total to $2.4 billion—up 22% from the same period last year. This performance exceeded our internal targets and positions us at the high end of the industry peer set, comparable to Lockheed Martin and RTX in their recent quarters.

Free cash flow came in at operating cash flow of $1.05 billion minus capital expenditures of $200 million. Our operating cash flow benefited from robust execution across core franchises: Aeronautics, Missiles & Fire Control, and Space Systems. Key drivers included favorable program timing on the F-35 Lightning II Joint Strike Fighter program, where we recognized $450 million in milestone payments from the U.S. DoD and international partners like the UK and Israel. We've also seen accelerated cash inflows from our hypersonic weapons portfolio, including the ARRW—Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon—analogous to Lockheed's efforts, which contributed $120 million this quarter amid heightened geopolitical demand.

Working capital management was a standout, with days sales outstanding improving to 45 days from 52 last year, thanks to disciplined collections on our $52 billion funded backlog—up 8% YoY. Inflation headwinds, which have plagued the sector with 5-7% cost escalation on fixed-price contracts like Boeing's T-7A trainer overruns, were mitigated through our Enterprise Cost Reduction Initiative, delivering $180 million in savings via lean manufacturing and supplier negotiations. FCF conversion from EBITDA now stands at 92%, a 300 basis point improvement, reflecting our shift toward higher-margin sustainment revenues, which grew 15% to $1.2 billion, driven by F-35 fleet upgrades and Patriot missile system logistics.

Regionally, U.S. government cash flows remain rock-solid, comprising 75% of our generation at $1.8 billion YTD, supported by the FY24 NDAA's $886 billion topline—though sequestration risks linger into FY25. Internationally, tailwinds from NATO's 2% GDP pledge brought $350 million in FCF from exports to Poland and Australia on HIMARS and JASSM lots. Middle East volumes were softer at $150 million due to delayed UAE THAAD deliveries amid supply chain bottlenecks in rare earths, but our localization efforts in the UAE—mirroring RTX's strategy—should unlock $200 million in accelerated cash next year.

On utilization, we're laser-focused on returning value to shareholders while investing for multi-year growth. Of our $2.4 billion YTD FCF, we deployed $1.1 billion to deleverage, reducing net debt to 1.8x EBITDA—below our 2.5x target and ahead of peers like Northrop Grumman. This included $600 million in term loan prepayments, lowering interest expense by 40 bps. Shareholder returns totaled $950 million: $450 million in dividends at our 1.8% yield, up 10% on the back of 15 years of consecutive increases, and $500 million in share repurchases under our $3 billion authorization, retiring 2.1 million shares or 1.2% of float at an average of $240 per share.

Strategically, we've earmarked $350 million for growth investments, including $150 million in capex for expanding our Camden, Arkansas hypersonics facility to support NGAD prototyping, and $100 million in digital twins and AI-driven predictive maintenance pilots across our F-35 sustainment ops. This aligns with industry trends toward Industry 4.0, reducing capex intensity from 8% of sales to 6% over three years. We've also completed two tuck-in acquisitions totaling $100 million: a directed energy firm in Colorado for $60 million to bolster our HELIOS laser program, and a space domain awareness startup for $40 million, positioning us against rising Chinese ASAT threats.

Looking forward, we expect FY24 FCF of $3.2 to $3.4 billion, implying 25% growth, with Q4 acceleration from LRIP-15 F-35 lots and Space Force EGS contracts. Risks include potential continuing resolutions delaying DoD disbursements and titanium supply volatility from Ukraine disruptions, but our $5 billion cash balance and undrawn $2 billion revolver provide ample dry powder. This FCF profile funds our 10-12% organic growth outlook through the decade and enables opportunistic M&A in cyber and unmanned systems, where valuations remain attractive at 12-14x EBITDA.

Finally, I'm thrilled with our standout performance on major new contract awards and program wins this quarter, underscoring the strength of our diversified portfolio across fixed-wing aircraft, missile defense, unmanned systems, and space domains. In Q3 alone, we secured $14.7 billion in funded bookings, bringing our year-to-date total to $42.3 billion—a 28% increase over the prior year and representing approximately 115% of our full-year revenue guidance. This bolsters our record backlog at $128 billion—up 17% YoY—and positions us for multi-year revenue visibility amid escalating global defense budgets.

U.S. programs accounted for 62% of Q3 bookings. First, our $6.2 billion IDIQ contract from the U.S. Air Force for Lot 18 production of the F-35 Lightning II Joint Strike Fighter, where Stratosphere Dynamics serves as the lead integrator for advanced avionics and electronic warfare suites. This includes $2.1 billion in funded orders for full-rate production deliveries starting in 2026, incorporating next-gen Block 4 upgrades with integrated AI-driven sensor fusion and directed energy weapon interfaces. Our win rate on F-35 task orders hit 72% this year, driven by our proprietary EagleEye mission data processing system, which reduces pilot workload by 35% in contested environments. This builds on our existing $18B F-35 backlog and aligns with the DoD's $849B FY25 budget request, prioritizing 5th-gen sustainment amid great power competition.

Complementing this, we captured a $3.8 billion sole-source contract under the NGAD risk reduction phase from DARPA and the Air Force Research Laboratory. Stratosphere Dynamics will lead digital engineering for collaborative combat aircraft—loyal wingman drones—integrating our hypersonic boost-glide vehicle prototypes with the program's digital twin architecture. Early flight tests at Edwards AFB demonstrated Mach 6+ sustained flight with 98% autonomy, positioning us ahead of competitors like Boeing and Northrop in this $100B+ decade-long opportunity. This win reflects our $1.2B annual R&D investment yielding a 4.2x ROI on tech transitions.

Shifting to missile defense, we won a $2.4 billion FMS award through the U.S. Army's Lower Tier Air and Missile Defense Sensor program, delivering next-gen Gallium Nitride-based radars to Poland and Romania as part of NATO's Eastern Flank enhancements. Funded value includes $900M for initial deployments by 2027, with serial production scaling to 150% of baseline rates. This leverages our integration with Raytheon's PAC-3 MSE interceptors, addressing hypersonic threats from peer adversaries—a market growing at 12% CAGR through 2030 per Teal Group forecasts.

Internationally, in the Middle East, we inked a $1.1 billion contract with the UAE for 48 Triton MQ-4C high-altitude ISR drones, plus sustainment, under the P-8 Poseidon family umbrella. This expands our UAE backlog to $4.5B and taps into Gulf Cooperation Council spending surges—up 22% YoY—fueled by Iran tensions and Red Sea disruptions.

In the Indo-Pacific, Australia selected us for a $650M tranche of the AUKUS Pillar II hypersonics initiative, co-developing scramjet-powered strike weapons compatible with the Loyal Wingman program. This positions us in the $20B+ AUKUS market, pursuing follow-on opportunities with Japan and South Korea amid China's J-20 expansions.

And in space, a $550M NRO contract for our NovaSat optical comms payloads on proliferated LEO constellations—think Starshield-adjacent architecture—supports resilient battlespace awareness. We're now at 85% domestic content on space wins, mitigating ITAR headwinds.

Strategically, these wins reflect our digital transformation—including MBSE and agile DevSecOps—boosting bid efficiency by 40%, enabling us to outpace incumbents on 70% of protested awards. International bookings hit 32% of Q3 total, up from 24% last year, driven by FMS multipliers and offset packages; we're targeting 40% by 2026 via hubs in Riyadh and Canberra. Amid FY25 DoD topline pressures from Ukraine aid and Taiwan contingencies, our focus on high-margin sustainment (65% program margins) and hypersonics (projected 25% EBITDA) de-risks the cycle. These awards validate our 'Fortress Portfolio' strategy—resilient across domains and geographies. We expect Q4 bookings of $10-12B, with full-year growth at the high end of our 15-20% guidance.

That covers the financial deep dive. Now over to Patricia for operations.

Patricia Gomez:
Thank you, Michael. Operationally, we have seen significant improvements in our supply chain management, allowing us to increase production rates on key programs like F-35 Lot 18 and hypersonic missiles. We are investing in automation and digital technologies to improve efficiency and reduce costs. Specifically, our 'China-plus-one' supplier strategy has derisked 92% of critical paths, cutting lead times by 25%, while our AeroSmart AI tool and Siemens Teamcenter PLM integration have boosted labor productivity by 18% and real-time forecasting accuracy.

Dr. Raj Singh:
Thank you, Patricia. On the technology front, we're making significant strides in our next-generation propulsion systems, including the XA102 adaptive cycle engine with 30% better TSFC and 25MW solid-state lasers validated in CENTCOM trials. We anticipate these advancements, along with hypersonic scramjets hitting Mach 12 and AI autonomy at 95% in CCA tests, will give us a competitive edge in the years to come. More specifically, our digital twins have de-risked NGAD Milestone B and JADC2 integration by 35%, positioning us for leadership in multi-domain operations.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. Our first question comes from Josh Klein with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Josh Klein:
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the program margins and cost performance analysis, particularly on the NGAD CPI?

Johnathan Reyes:
Certainly, Josh. As Michael detailed, NGAD margins hit 11.5% with a CPI of 1.12, driven by digital twin risk retirement and additive manufacturing savings on titanium components—15% unit cost reduction. This outperforms our portfolio average and sets up LRIP upside in Q4, despite industry-wide inflation.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Maria Lopez with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Maria Lopez:
Hi, thanks. I'm curious about the revenue and earnings guidance by segment, especially Missiles & Fire Control growth drivers?

Michael Lang:
Maria, great question. Missiles & Fire Control guides to $28-30 billion, up 15-20%, on 4,500-5,000 deliveries including JASSM-ER and PAC-3 MSE at 120/month rates by Q4. Margins expand to 14.5-15.0% from scale and international NATO demand up 25%, fueled by Ukraine replenishment and Taiwan tensions.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Kim with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

David Kim:
Regarding the R&D investment in next-generation platforms and technologies, how are you prioritizing hypersonics versus CCA?

Dr. Raj Singh:
